source_text: aliam illi regulam praetendo: sicut naturalia, ita rationalia esse debere in deo omnia. exigo rationem bonitatis, quia nec aliud quid bonum haberi liceat, quod non rationaliter bonum sit, nedum ut ipsa bonitas inrationalis deprehendatur. facilius malum, cui rationis aliquid adfuerit, pro bono habebitur quam ut bonum ratone desertum non pro malo iudicetur. nego rationalem bonitatem\', dei Marcionis iam hoc primo, quod in salutem processerit; hominis alieni. scio dicturos atquin hanc esse principalem \' et perfectam bonitatem, cum sine ullo debito familiaritatis iri extraneos uoluntaria et libera effundatur, secundum quam inimicos quoque nostros et hoc nomine iam extraneos diligere iubeamur. cur ergo non a primordio hominem respexit. a primordio extraneum? cessando praeiudicauit cum extraneo nihil sibi esse. ceterum disciplinam diligendi extraneum uel inimicum antecessit praeceptum diligendi proximum tamquam te ipsum. quod etsi ex lege creatoris, et tu quoque illud excipere debebis, ut a Christo non destructum, sed potius exstructum. nam quo magis proximum diligas, diligere iuberis inimicum et extraneum. exaggeratio est debitae bonitatis exactio indebitae. antecedit autem debita indebitam, ut principalis, ut dignior, ut ministra et comite sua [id est indebita] prior. igitur cum prima bonitatis ratio sit in rem suam exhiberi ex iustitia, secunda autem in alienam ex redundantia iustitiae super scribarum et Pharisaeorum, quale est secundam ei rationem referri, cui deficit prima, non habenti proprium hominem ac per hoc quoque exiguae? porro exigua, quae suum non habuit, quomodo in alienum redundauit? exhibe principalem rationem, et tunc uindica sequentem. nulla res sine ordine rationalis potest uindicari; tanto abest, ut ratio ipsa in aliquo ordinem amittat. sit nunc et a secundo gradu incipiens ratio bonitatis, in extraneum scilicet: nec secundus illi gradus ratione constabit, alio modo destructus. tunc enim rationalis habebitur uel secunda in extraneum bonitas, si sine iniuria eius operetur, cuius est res. quamcumque bonitatem iustitia prima efficit rationalem. sicut in principali gradu, cum in rem suam exhibetur, rationalis erit si iusta sit, sic et in extraneum rationalis uideri poterit, si non sit iniusta. ceterum qualis bonitas quae per iniuriam constat, et quidem pro extraneo? fortasse enim pro domestico aliquatenus rationalis habeatur bonitas iniuriosa. pro extraneo uero, cui nec proba legitime deberetur, qua ratione tam iniusta rationalis defendetur? quid enim iniustius, quid iniquius et improbius quam ita alieno benefacere seruo, ut domino eripiatur, ut alii uindicetur, ut aduersus caput domini subornetur, et quidem, quod indignius, in ipsa adhuc domo domini, de ipsius adhuc horreis uiuens, sub ipsius adhuc plagis tremens? talis adsertor etiam damnaretur in saeculo, nedum plagiator. non aliter ** deus Marcionis, inrumpens in alienum mundum, eripiens deo hominem, patri filium, educatori aluminum, domino famulum, ut eum efficiat deo impium, patri inreligiosum, educatori ingratum, domino nequam. oro te, si rationalis bonitas talem facit, qualem faceret inrationalis? non putem impudentiorem quam qui in aliena aqua alii deo tingitur, ad alienum caelum alii deo expanditur, in aliena terra alii deo sternitur, super alienum panem alii deo gratiarum actionibus fungitur, de alienis bonis ob alium deum nomine elemosynae et dilectionis operatur. quis iste deus tam bonus, ut homo ab illo malus fiat, tam propitius, ut alium illi deum, et dominum quidem ipsius, faciat iratum?
pass_a_gloss: I propose to him another rule: just as natural things, so also rational things ought to be in God. I demand a reason for goodness, because no other thing can be considered good unless it is rationally good, and certainly not that goodness itself is irrational. It is easier for evil, to which some reason has been added, to be considered good than for good, deserted by reason, not to be judged as evil. I deny rational goodness to Marcion's God, first because he proceeded to the salvation of a foreign man; I know they will say that this is the principal and perfect goodness, because it is voluntarily and freely poured out on foreigners without any debt of familiarity, according to which we are also commanded to love our enemies, who are already foreigners by this name. Why, therefore, did he not regard man from the beginning, from the beginning a foreigner? By ceasing, he prejudged that he had nothing to do with the foreigner. Moreover, the discipline of loving a foreigner or enemy preceded the command to love one's neighbor as oneself. Which, although it is from the law of the Creator, you also ought to accept, so that it is not destroyed by Christ, but rather built upon. For the more you love your neighbor, the more you are commanded to love your enemy and foreigner. The exacting of debt is an exaggeration of owed goodness. But owed goodness precedes unowed goodness, as principal, as more worthy, as minister and companion to its own, that is, unowed goodness, prior. Therefore, when the first reason for goodness is to exhibit it to one's own from justice, and the second is to exhibit it to a foreigner from the abundance of justice, what kind of second reason can be attributed to one who lacks the first, and does not have his own man, and therefore is also deficient? Furthermore, what is deficient, which did not have its own, how did it overflow into a foreigner? Show the principal reason, and then vindicate the subsequent one. No thing can be vindicated without order; so much so that reason itself does not lose order in anything. Let the reason for goodness now begin from the second degree, namely, in a foreigner: nor will the second degree of goodness be consistent with reason, having been destroyed in another way. For then rational goodness will be considered, or second goodness in a foreigner, if it operates without injury to him whose thing it is. Whatever goodness justice first effects is rational. Just as in the principal degree, when it is exhibited to one's own, it will be rational if it is just, so also in a foreigner it can be seen as rational if it is not unjust. But what kind of goodness is it that consists through injury, and indeed for a foreigner? Perhaps, indeed, goodness that is injurious can be considered rational for a domestic servant. But for a foreigner, to whom not even legitimate goodness is owed, by what reason can such unjust goodness be defended? What is more unjust, more iniquitous, and more wicked than to do good to a foreign servant in such a way that it is taken away from the master, that it is vindicated to another, that it is suborned against the head of the master, and indeed, what is more indignation, in the very house of the master, living from the master's stores, trembling under the master's blows? Such a defender would even be condemned in the world, not to mention the plagiarist. Not otherwise does Marcion's God, bursting into a foreign world, taking man away from God, son away from father, pupil away from educator, servant away from master, so that he makes him impious to God, irreligious to father, ungrateful to educator, wicked to master. I ask you, if rational goodness makes such a person, what would irrational goodness make? I do not think there is anyone more shameless than one who is baptized in another's water to another god, who expands to another god in another's heaven, who is laid out on another's earth to another god, who performs thanksgiving actions to another god over another's bread, who works with another's goods in the name of elemosynae and love for another god. What kind of god is so good that man becomes evil from him, so propitious that he makes another god, and indeed the master of him, angry?
pass_b_english: I am setting another rule before him: just as natural things are rational, so everything in God must be rational. I demand a reason for goodness, because nothing else can count as good unless it is rationally good, let alone that goodness itself should be caught being irrational. It is easier for evil with some reason attached to pass for good than for good, deserted by reason, to escape being judged evil. I deny rational goodness to Marcion's God—first of all, because he proceeded to save a foreign man. I know they will claim this is the principal and perfect goodness, since it is poured out voluntarily and freely on foreigners without any debt of familiarity—according to which we are commanded to love even our enemies, who are already foreigners by that very name. Why, then, did he not regard man from the beginning, a foreigner from the beginning? By holding back, he prejudged that he had nothing to do with the foreigner. Moreover, the discipline of loving a foreigner or enemy came before the command to love your neighbor as yourself. Even though that command comes from the Creator's law, you must accept it too, so that it is not destroyed by Christ but rather built upon. For the more you love your neighbor, the more you are commanded to love your enemy and the foreigner. Exacting what is owed is an exaggeration of owed goodness. But owed goodness comes before unowed goodness—as principal, as more worthy, as minister and companion to its own, that is, unowed goodness, which is prior. So when the first reason for goodness is to show it to one's own out of justice, and the second is to show it to a foreigner out of the overflow of justice, what kind of second reason can be assigned to one who lacks the first, who does not have his own man, and is therefore deficient even in the lesser? Furthermore, how did what is deficient, which never had its own, overflow into a foreigner? Produce the principal reason, and only then vindicate the subsequent one. Nothing can be vindicated without rational order; so much so that reason itself never loses order in anything. Let the reason for goodness now begin from the second degree, that is, toward a foreigner: nor will that second degree of goodness hold together with reason, having been destroyed in another way. For only then will the second goodness toward a foreigner be considered rational if it operates without injury to him whose property it is. Whatever goodness justice first produces is rational. Just as in the principal degree, when it is shown to one's own, it will be rational if it is just, so also toward a foreigner it can appear rational if it is not unjust. But what kind of goodness consists through injury, and that for a foreigner? Perhaps injurious goodness might be considered rational for a household member. But for a foreigner, to whom not even legitimate goodness is owed, by what reason can such unjust goodness be defended? What is more unjust, more iniquitous, more wicked than to benefit a foreign servant in such a way that he is taken from his master, vindicated to another, suborned against his master's head—and what is more outrageous—right in the master's own house, living off the master's own stores, trembling under the master's own blows? Such a defender would be condemned even in the world, let alone the plagiarist. Marcion's God acts no differently: bursting into a foreign world, snatching man from God, son from father, pupil from educator, servant from master, so that he makes him impious toward God, irreligious toward his father, ungrateful toward his educator, wicked toward his master. I ask you: if rational goodness produces such a person, what would irrational goodness produce? I cannot imagine anyone more shameless than the one who is baptized in another's water for another god, who expands toward another god in another's heaven, who is laid out on another's earth for another god, who offers thanksgiving over another's bread to another god, who works with another's goods in the name of alms and love for another god. What kind of god is so good that man becomes evil through him, so favorable that he makes another god—indeed, that god's own master—angry?

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex logical structure of Tertullian's argument regarding the 'rationality' of goodness and the critique of Marcion's God. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Latin source. All clauses, including the rhetorical questions and the list of thefts (man from God, son from father, etc.), are preserved. The distinction between 'debita' (owed) and 'indebita' (unowed/not due) is correctly handled.
